questions.q: What credentials does an IAM user have, per this lesson?
options: Long-term credentials — a console password, access keys, or both — that don't expire on their own
No credentials at all; users can only be assumed like roles
Only a temporary session token that expires after one hour
A single shared password used by the entire AWS account
questions.explain: IAM users carry long-term credentials, which is exactly what makes leaked ones dangerous — they stay valid until manually revoked.

questions.q: What is an IAM group, precisely?
options: A named collection of users used to attach policies once instead of per-user — it is not an identity and has no credentials
An identity that can be assumed by a Lambda function
A synonym for an IAM role with a different name
A billing construct that has nothing to do with permissions
questions.explain: Groups are purely administrative — a container for users, never something logged into or assumed.

questions.q: Why does an IAM role use temporary credentials instead of long-term ones?
options: Because a role is assumed rather than owned — whoever assumes it gets short-lived credentials via AWS STS that expire automatically, reducing what a leak could expose
Because temporary credentials are easier for AWS to bill
Because roles are only usable for exactly one API call ever
Roles actually do use long-term credentials, identical to users
questions.explain: Temporary, auto-expiring credentials are the core security advantage roles have over users for anything automated.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why should a Glue job assume an IAM role rather than run on an IAM user's access key?
options: The role's credentials are temporary and scoped to the job's runtime, so there's nothing long-lived to leak; a hardcoded user access key is a standing secret sitting in a script
Glue jobs are technically incapable of using IAM users at all
Access keys are more expensive to use than role-based credentials
There is no real difference — it's purely a stylistic choice
questions.explain: This is the central data-engineering reason to prefer roles: temporary, auto-expiring credentials versus a long-lived leakable secret.

questions.q: What does a role have attached to it that a user or group does not?
options: A trust policy, which defines who or what is allowed to assume the role
A billing alarm that users and groups can never have
A permanent password that never rotates
A VPC endpoint bound directly to the role
questions.explain: A role carries both a permissions policy (what it can do) and a trust policy (who can assume it) — users and groups have no trust policy.
